scope: Initial catalogue definitions and tier variants; no live users or encounter state. Stat prose is not uniformly automated.

records.f: The first thing they teach you is to lead the target. The second is to stop thinking of the rounds as individual shots. At combat rates, you're not shooting at a machine so much as painting a region of space with metal and asking the other pilot to make one mistake.

records.f: There is a satisfying finality to a thirty-millimeter impact. No warning tone, no shimmering barrier, no exotic energy signature for the analysts to argue about afterward. Just a tremendous noise, a shower of armor fragments, and a maintenance officer asking why the ammunition expenditure exceeds the mission allotment by six hundred percent.

records.f: It spins up like a turbine and empties like a promise. Every Rebel cell wants one, and the ones who have one want more ammunition.

You can tell when a pilot has started believing their own reputation. They stop closing distance, start posing for their gun cameras, and think the big gun makes them untouchable. Then someone with an ordinary rifle catches them between shots. A hand cannon is a wonderful tool. It is not a personality.

records.f: Rebel mechanics call it a door-knocker. The door, in practice, is the back of a knight.

records.f: A good rifle doesn't need to be impressive. It needs to do the same thing every time you pull the trigger. We built this one to punch through the front plate of a heavy chassis at a range where the other fellow is still deciding whether you're a sensor ghost. If you can keep the barrel steady, the rest is arithmetic.

records.f: The rookies love rockets because they can put a dozen little suns between themselves and the enemy, then call it marksmanship. The veterans love them for what comes afterward: the split formation, the broken rhythm, the instant when a proud ace must choose between holding their ground and living long enough to fight again.

records.f: Same rocket as the pod in a bigger rack, fired in two salvos, with none of the glamour. Line regiments like it because a second salvo is a second chance.

records.f: There is an art to forcing a knight from their chosen ground, and few tools are as honest about it as a well-placed salvo. The rockets need not kill the enemy; they need only make him turn, make him brake, make him abandon the perfect firing line he spent the last thirty seconds preparing.

records.f: No ace is foolish enough to stand still when a 120mm salvo paints the sky above them; the warning arrives, the thrusters flare, and the dance begins.

Rookies trust the gun because it lets them kill a man without ever having to meet his eyes. A blade is different; it demands you understand your machine, your opponent, and the distance between their next breath and your next movement.

A rifle lets you fight the enemy you see; a blade forces you to feel the enemy you face. Every movement carries intent, every clash tells a story, and somewhere between the first parry and the final cut, the machine ceases to be steel and servo and becomes an extension of the soul.

Nobody sensible wants to duel a heavy blade. The weapon is too expensive, the risk is too great, and there are a dozen more efficient ways to destroy a chassis. Unfortunately, battlefields are not arranged by sensible people. Someone will always run out of ammunition, lose a weapon arm, or decide that getting close is preferable to being shot at from across a kilometer.

records.x: 1 pile cartridge, reload after each shot
records.f: A pile bunker is not a duelist's weapon. It is a decision made one turn in advance and paid for in full the moment it lands. The charge whine tells everyone on the field what is coming, and the pilot who wastes it learns how long a reload takes with an enemy still standing. The pilot who connects does not need a second shot.

A shield is not supposed to stop everything. That's a child's understanding of the word. Its job is to turn the one shot you couldn't dodge into the one shot you can survive. If you come back with a shattered shield and an intact cockpit, it has performed admirably.

The first time I took a direct hit on the shield, I thought the cockpit had split open. Every alarm went off at once, and the whole frame slewed sideways hard enough to throw up my dinner. Then the damage report came in. Minor actuator strain, shield integrity down forty percent, pilot condition stable. I started laughing. Couldn't stop for nearly a minute.

For all the arguments about maneuverability, thrust-to-weight ratios, and the superiority of the first strike, the large shield remains one of the few pieces of equipment whose value can be demonstrated with a single photograph: the pilot standing beside a wrecked machine, helmet under one arm, looking confused about still being alive.

The unit commander ordered us to advance behind the shield line, and for the first time that morning I felt safe. Not confident. Not brave. Safe. The machines moved forward through a hail of fire, their shields grinding sparks from the concrete, and we followed in their shadow. I used to think of courage as moving toward danger. That day I learned it could also mean having something between you and it.

Every additional plate brings a compromise. Mass, actuator load, thermal retention, maintenance hours. The sales brochure calls this package a survivability enhancement, which is accurate in much the same way that a bunker is a survivability enhancement. The question is whether your frame can still get to the fight before the enemy finishes it.

Shaped charges are ingenious things. They take a small amount of explosive and ask geometry to do the rest. Spaced armor answers with a rather unscientific objection: the jet does not get to arrive at the target in the condition its designers intended. Against kinetic penetrators, it offers considerably less consolation. Engineering is full of such compromises.

The panel did exactly what it was designed to do. It broke apart, distributed the impact, and gave up its entire existence to save the arm underneath. The pilot called it a lucky hit. The maintenance chief called it a replacement order. Both were right, and the arm was still attached.

The pod buys you one attack's worth of confusion. That's it. No magical invisibility, no permanent bubble of safety, no guarantee that the next missile will miss. Just a brief interruption in the enemy's certainty at precisely the moment they were counting on it. In the hands of a good pilot, that is enough. In the hands of a bad one, it's an expensive way to be surprised twice.

It looks ridiculous until you've watched a light frame cross a kilometer of paved industrial road before the enemy has finished setting up their firing positions. Then it looks ridiculous and effective, which is a category of military equipment the procurement officers have never fully understood.

Boosters don't make you faster. They make you fast at a time when you desperately need to be. The trick is remembering that momentum has a price, heat has a price, and the enemy gets a vote in what happens when you finish your burn. Every rookie wants to fly. Every veteran wants to know where they'll be when the thrust runs out.

There is a special kind of silence just after a jump, when the ground has fallen away and your frame is committed to a trajectory you can no longer alter with your feet. For a moment, the alarms, the radio, the gunfire, all of it seems to vanish. Then the landing computer starts screaming at you, and you remember that gravity has been waiting patiently the whole time.

There is a persistent misconception that a targeting computer makes a mediocre pilot dangerous. It does not. What it does is remove a handful of small, stupid errors between deciding to shoot and putting a round through the part of the enemy that matters. At the highest levels, a handful of small, stupid errors is the difference between an ace and a casualty statistic.

Recoil is predictable. That is the whole point of the system. Your weapon kicks, the frame compensates, the next firing solution is calculated, and the cycle repeats. Unfortunately, your opponent is not predictable, your footing may be terrible, and the arm you're using to mount a weapon that weighs as much as a transport vehicle has already taken two hits. Technology is wonderful. It is not a substitute for knowing when to stop shooting.

You don't notice the gyros when they're working. You notice them when they aren't. The sights wander, the frame leans into the recoil, and the whole machine begins to feel like it's standing on a moving deck. Then you realize the gyro warning has been blinking for thirty seconds, and the last time you saw a maintenance window was four sorties ago.

The first casualty of electronic warfare is certainty. Your sensors report an empty street, your targeting computer insists something moved through your blind spot, and command wants to know why you haven't engaged the hostile that everyone else can apparently see. You begin to understand that the battlefield is not what you observe. It is what you can prove.

We had a clean return, full profile, heat signature, estimated mass, the lot. For about three seconds, we were very pleased with ourselves. Then the enemy switched on their countermeasures and our beautiful picture dissolved into a thousand plausible lies. The lesson isn't that sensors are useless. It's that knowing something is there and knowing what it is are two very different military achievements.

records.r: Holding the line after heavy hits
records.f: Imperial doctrine assumes the arm will be hit. The harness assumes the pilot still needs it afterward.
The gun cameras show three of them. The wreckage shows one. Fox-spirit tricks, the Reman pilots call it, and they bow before switching it on.
The fastest rig our test pilots have flown, and the only one that came back from trials in more pieces than it left with.

records.f: Imperial knights were never meant to dance. Plant the spades, and the line holds.

records.r: Long patrols, siege endurance, heavy draw
records.f: Oleum Vis does not run out. The pilots do. Imperial crews rotate on dosimeter, not on fuel state.
Imperial thrusters are tuned to last a century. Rebel stacks are tuned to last until the next depot.
Reman pilots say the suite doesn't see the target; it lets the pilot see it. Our technicians reported a headache and declined to elaborate.

records.f: Every Musha we've recovered came with its pilot's name lacquered inside the cockpit. Our mechanics stopped scraping it off after the third one wouldn't start.

records.s: ST/HP:160 DR:450/300 MOVE:2L/- SM:+5 HND:0 SR:5
records.f: The Crawler has outlived three dynasties and two of its replacements. It will probably outlive us.
The maul was meant to retire with the old foot knights. It refused. A knight on the ground is a knight out of the fight, and nothing puts one there faster.

records.f: Pieced together from a downed Reman lance and three civilian mining rigs. It works. Nobody knows for how long.
Reman blades go through our best plate like paper, and the edge never seems to dull. We have stopped asking how.

records.f: Shadow-children, the Reman pilots call them. Four small guns, one mind, and no safe facing anywhere on the field.

records.r: Heat-limited heavy blocking at low mass
records.f: A Reman beam shield weighs less than our bucklers and blocks like our tower walls. Our engineers have measured the field three times and stopped believing the readings.

records.r: Durable armor with a supply chain
records.f: Every plate is lacquered by hand at a temple-foundry. Captured suits rust within a season. We have tried six lacquers.
Shukuchi: shrinking the earth. It is there on the sensor, and then it is five meters to the left and smiling.
Tsukuroi: mending. The swarm repairs a wound the way a monk repairs a robe, slowly and with great care.

records.s: ST/HP:200 DR:800/400 MOVE:5L/10S SM:+7 HND:0 SR:3
records.f: Castellans are older than most noble houses and better maintained. They do not charge; they arrive.

records.f: The carrier has no glory and no enemies; nobody bothers to shoot it until it has already unloaded.

records.s: ST/HP:65 DR:150/80 MOVE:8L/- SM:+3 HND:+3 SR:2 CREW:driver_and_gunner
records.f: A cargo truck, a welded mount and a gunner with nothing to lose. Rebels field more of these than knights.

records.s: ST/HP:140 DR:480/300 MOVE:6L/- SM:+4 HND:+2 SR:3 CREW:driver_gunner_commander NOTE:Locomotion_disabled_halves_MOVE_instead_of_stopping_it NOTE:High_Maintenance_-2_to_repair_rolls
records.f: It crosses rivers our tanks must bridge and fields our tanks must bypass. Its lift fans, thankfully, are made of cloth-weave and pride.
Tamashii: soul. The core hums a note that Reman engineers tune by ear. Imperial jammers, it turns out, sing off-key.
Kaze-no-mai: wind dance. The jets turn the knight the way a fan turns in a dancer's hand.

ECM SUITE: A jammer pack flooding nearby bands with noise. Good for close cover.
Vehicle-grade noise that blankets a firebase-sized area.
Fixed-station grade: the whole battlefield hisses with static.
SENSOR SUITE: A compact radar and thermal head mount, a scout favorite.
A retractable mast for spotters and command frames.
A back-mounted dish: the battlefield's eyes.
